turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, thank you. Well, what finally pushed me to come in is... it's work, mostly. I manage a health clinic, and I'll sit down to do an EPIC quality report. Which, honestly, they just updated the EPIC system again last month and the new interface is just a total nightmare. The dashboard colors are completely different now, and my whole team has been complaining about it. Susan—she's my lead nurse—was just telling me yesterday how it actually gives her a headache to look at it for too long. 

But anyway, I'll start the report, or I'll sit down in a clinic metrics meeting with every intention of tracking the data, and within a few minutes my mind has drifted so far off. I end up just rereading the exact same numbers over and over, or I'll suddenly realize I completely missed the whole point of the discussion.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly describes an inability to sustain attention during tasks like reports or meetings, noting their mind drifts off within minutes and they have to reread information.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had trouble focusing like this since you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, actually. Even way back in elementary school... I remember my teachers were always writing on my report cards that I was, you know, "bright but careless." Which is such a funny word to use, careless. My third-grade teacher, Mrs. Higgins, she wrote that on everything in this bright green felt-tip pen she always used. She was completely obsessed with the color green. She even drove this awful mint-green station wagon. Actually, I saw a station wagon just like it the other day when I was at the grocery store, which you just never see anymore! Everyone only drives SUVs now. It was parked right next to the cart return, and I remember thinking how hard it must be to find parts for those old cars if they break down... 

But, um... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, being a kid. Yeah, so my mother actually had to sit right next to me at the kitchen table every single night just to make sure I finished my homework. Because if she didn't, I would completely lose track of what the assignments even were. Or we'd sit down and I'd realize I forgot my textbooks at school again. Which drove her absolutely crazy, but to be fair, those cubbies they gave us were so incredibly small, you could barely fit a winter coat in them, let alone all those heavy books...

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient reports that their elementary school teachers frequently noted they made careless mistakes, describing them as 'bright but careless.'
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient states they would fail to finish their homework and lose track of assignments unless their mother sat with them to ensure completion.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions frequently forgetting their textbooks at school, which are necessary items for completing their homework.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts during the interview, going off on a tangent about a station wagon and losing their train of thought.

turns.doctor_question: Do these focus problems cause you to make mistakes or miss important things at work or in daily life?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, unfortunately, they really do. Like at work, my delays have started affecting our clinic reporting deadlines, which ends up making the other teams wait on me. The billing department is usually the one waiting, and Carol in billing—she’s been there for twenty years. Actually, her work anniversary was just last week and they got her this huge ice cream cake. I can’t eat ice cream much anymore, though, dairy just really bothers my stomach now that I'm fifty. I tried that oat milk ice cream instead, but it just has this weird texture, you know? It's kind of chalky and it doesn't melt the same way in your bowl. 

But anyway, making the other teams wait on me is just... it's embarrassing. And it's happening outside of work, too. I’ve actually had to step back from leading parts of the volunteer health workshops I do. We hold them at the community center downtown, the one with the really beautiful old brick facade. They just renovated the lobby and put in these gorgeous skylights. It’s so nice, except I heard they already have a leak, which is just typical, right? Contractors these days charge an absolute fortune and then they completely rush the job. My neighbor had to get her roof done last spring and the scaffolding was up for months, it killed all her hydrangeas... um... 

Wait, sorry. The workshops. Yeah, I just had to step back because I can’t reliably keep all the planning pieces moving anymore. There are just too many moving parts and I keep dropping them.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly confirms the doctor's question about their focus problems causing them to make mistakes or miss important things.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes failing to finish workplace duties on time, causing delays in clinic reporting deadlines and making other teams wait.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient states they had to step back from leading workshops because they cannot organize or 'keep all the planning pieces moving' and keep dropping them.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts during the conversation, going on long tangents about ice cream, lactose intolerance, building renovations, and a neighbor's roof before catching themselves.

turns.doctor_question: When you’re trying to focus, are you usually distracted by excessive worry?
turns.patient_response:
No, not really. It's not like I'm sitting there worrying about things. I mean, everyone has worries, obviously, like retirement savings. My husband was just saying the other day that we need to rebalance our 401k because the market's been so volatile lately. Which is so frustrating because I feel like every time we try to get ahead, something happens with the economy. Like when we bought our first house back in the late nineties, the interest rates were just ridiculous. We had this tiny little starter home with a bright yellow front door. I loved that door. I wanted to paint our current door yellow, but the homeowner's association here is so strict. They have a pre-approved color palette and it's literally just six shades of beige. Who wants a beige door? It's so depressing. 

But, um, no, it's not worry that distracts me. It's more like my brain just... turns off, or wanders away to something else entirely, like the beige doors, I guess. I just sort of space out.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes their brain wandering away to unrelated thoughts, demonstrating distractibility.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient explicitly denies being distracted by worry or sitting around worrying about things.
symptom_reasoning.S059: The patient states that their brain 'turns off' and they 'space out' when trying to focus, which aligns with the mind going blank.

turns.doctor_question: Have you been feeling down or depressed most days recently?
turns.patient_response:
No, I wouldn't say I've been feeling depressed. I mean, I have days where I'm tired, but who doesn't? Working in healthcare management is just exhausting right now. The regulations change every five minutes, and trying to keep the staff scheduled is a nightmare. Our head nurse, Sarah, she just went out on maternity leave, which is wonderful for her, of course. She's having a little girl. They did one of those gender reveal things with a cake, where you cut into it and the frosting inside is pink or blue. I always think those are a little silly, honestly. When I had my kids, we just waited until they were born to find out. It was a surprise! My oldest, Michael, he was almost ten pounds when he was born. The nurses couldn't believe it. He's still tall, he actually just started a new job in Chicago... 

But, um, anyway, what were you asking? Oh, feeling down. No, I don't think I'm depressed. I just get frustrated with myself when I can't keep things straight, but I'm not sad all the time or anything like that.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, going on a long tangent about a coworker, gender reveal cakes, and her son before forgetting the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly denies feeling depressed or being sad all the time.

turns.doctor_question: Have you often found yourself acting impulsively, like interrupting others or making decisions without thinking them through?
turns.patient_response:
No, I don't really think so. I'm not much of an interrupter. Actually, my husband is the one who interrupts all the time, especially when we're watching TV. We were watching this new mystery series on streaming the other night—the one set in Scotland, with all those gorgeous sweeping shots of the highlands. I've always wanted to go to Scotland. My grandmother was Scottish, well, half Scottish. She used to make this incredible shortbread at Christmas. Real butter, none of that margarine nonsense. You can always taste the difference when people use cheap butter in baking. I tried to make her recipe last year, but my oven runs hot, so the bottoms got a little too brown. It's a gas oven, and I swear the temperature dial is just a suggestion at this point. We really need to get a new stove, but the appliance store down the street closed, and now you have to drive all the way out to the big box store on the highway, and the traffic out there is just horrendous on the weekends... 

Um, but no, I don't think I'm impulsive. I usually overthink things, if anything.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response demonstrates tangentiality, wandering through a chain of loosely related topics (TV shows, Scotland, baking, ovens, traffic) before returning to the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly denies being an interrupter.

turns.doctor_question: Did these concentration problems also happen when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, actually. Even way back in elementary school. I remember my teachers were always writing on my report cards that I was bright but careless. My mother was so frustrated by it. She used to have to sit with me at the kitchen table every single night just to make sure I finished my homework. I was always losing track of my assignments, or I'd leave my math book at school. We had these heavy, awful textbooks back then, the ones with the glossy covers that always got bent at the corners. I remember my science book had a picture of a space shuttle on it. It was right around the time the Challenger happened, which was just so awful. We all watched it on those big boxy TVs they'd roll into the classroom on a metal cart. You know, the ones with the VCR strapped to the bottom? I wonder whatever happened to all those carts. They were so squeaky. Our janitor, Mr. Henderson, he was always trying to oil the wheels but it never worked. He was a sweet man, though. He used to give us extra cartons of chocolate milk on Fridays if we helped him stack the chairs...

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, being a kid. Yeah, my mom had to sit with me because I'd just forget everything. So it's definitely been an issue for a long time.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient recalls teachers writing on report cards that they were 'careless.'
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient notes their mother had to sit with them every night to ensure they finished their homework.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient describes frequently losing track of assignments and leaving their math book at school.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by going on a long tangent about textbooks, TVs, and a janitor, eventually losing their train of thought.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient explicitly states that as a child they would 'just forget everything.'
symptom_reasoning.S031: The patient confirms the doctor's question about having 'concentration problems' since childhood.
